title: The teachers you met
hook: Marcus, Rumi, Epictetus, Zhuangzi, Julian, the Kotzker Rebbe

segments.voice: Yesterday: the practices you kept. Your line was what survived. Which two did you choose, and did both happen today, even small? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

Nearly two thousand years ago, the most powerful man in the world sat down to write in his private notebook. He was the emperor of Rome, and the first thing he wrote wasn't a plan or a law. It was a list of thank-yous. From my grandfather, good manners and an even temper. From my mother, generosity, and a simple way of living. From one teacher, not to take sides at the chariot races. From another, to put up with hard work and want little. Page after page. Before Marcus Aurelius wrote a single thought of his own, he named where each one came from. Today, we do the same: the teachers you met.
screen: `THE EMPEROR'S PRIVATE NOTEBOOK.` → `PAGE ONE: THANK-YOUS.` → `WHERE EACH ONE CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Let's walk the line of them, one at a time, each in their own house. First, the Stoics. Marcus, arguing with himself under the blankets, then writing the Meditations, whose Greek title means simply to himself. Epictetus, enslaved as a young man, who warned his master he'd break his leg and, when it broke, said only: didn't I tell you? He taught that some things are in our power and some aren't. Second, the mystics of the heart. Rumi, the Persian poet whose Masnavi opens with a reed flute crying for the reed bed it was cut from, the song of every soul that misses home. And Julian of Norwich, an English anchoress who lived in a single room attached to a church, saw all that is made as small as a hazelnut in her palm, and wrote down what she heard in her visions. In Grace Warrack's translation: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Third, the tricksters of the way. Zhuangzi, the Chinese sage who dreamed he was a butterfly and woke unsure which one was dreaming, and who argued on a bridge about whether anyone can know the joy of fish. Fourth, the fierce ones. The Kotzker Rebbe, a Hasidic master in nineteenth-century Poland, famous for his impatience with anything fake. Asked where God lives, the story goes, he answered: wherever people let God in. None of them agreed on everything. Some would have argued fiercely with each other. That's why we left each in their own house. But every one of them handed you something, the way Marcus's teachers handed him an even temper. Naming it is the thank-you.
screen: `MARCUS AND EPICTETUS.` · `RUMI AND JULIAN.` · `ZHUANGZI AND THE BUTTERFLY.` · `THE KOTZKER: LET IT IN.` · then, large: `THANK THE TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Pick one teacher from this year. One of these, or another you met along the way. Now finish Marcus's sentence for yourself, silently: from this teacher, I learned. One thing. Keep it simple, the way he did. Then, if you like, write it down as a short thank-you note, to someone who can't read it. You're naming where it came from. The bell holds the time.
The teachers you met. Marcus, Epictetus, Rumi, Julian, Zhuangzi, the Kotzker Rebbe: each in their own house, each handing you something. Today's word.
Your line: thank the teachers. Write one line today, the way Marcus did: from this person, I learned this. A living teacher counts too. Maybe tell them. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

notes: Meditations I: grandfather Verus (good morals, government of temper), mother (piety, beneficence, simplicity of living), tutor (not to be a partisan of the Green or Blue at the races; to endure labor, want little). Paraphrased; confirm the hook's order and wording.
Julian, Warrack 1901, ch. 27 (Thirteenth Revelation): confirm exact wording.
Kotzker 'wherever people let God in' is an oral Hasidic tradition (told on day 63); 'the story goes' used.
